body: #### **The first week of June brings a focus on food security, water sustainability, energy policy, and economic performance across the Middle East and North Africa. From international conferences in Cairo and Abu Dhabi to key economic data releases in Türkiye and a closely watched OPEC+ ministerial meeting, governments and policymakers will be assessing both immediate challenges and long-term development priorities.**. The blue logo of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) is displayed on the facade of its headquarters building in Vienna, Austria, on June 9, 2025. Cairo will host the FoodGuard Global Summit from 2–4 June, bringing together policymakers, industry leaders, researchers, and international organizations to address food loss and waste across Africa and the Middle East. Abu Dhabi will host the MENA Dams Conference on 3–4 June, convening water authorities, engineers, and infrastructure specialists from across the region. At the same time, 2025 marked the return of Donald Trump and the United States as a central actor in the Middle East. From investment-driven agreements with Gulf countries to renewed efforts at normalisation with Syria, and culminating in strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities as well as a leading role in the Gaza peace plan, the year confirmed **Washington’s renewed capacity to project power and influence** across the region. With elections scheduled in Morocco, Algeria, Lebanon and, most notably, Israel, alongside major multilateral gatherings such as COP31 in Antalya, the MENA region is once again set to **be at the centre of international attention**. “In 2026, the Arab Middle East and North Africa (MENA) may be less permeable than a decade ago – but also more fragile.
